message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after you notify the landlord. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (no more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The lease ends automatically unless renewed.
• **Early termination**: Some leases allow early termination for a fee; otherwise, you may be liable for rent until the end of the term. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or disturbances to the landlord in writing. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and request a written explanation if you suspect unlawful entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the repair and the amount deducted. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** before raising rent.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent increases are only allowed at the start of a new lease term. | • Review the lease and negotiate if you anticipate a rent hike. | | **Eviction** | • The landlord must provide a **written notice** (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violations, 60 days for no‑cause eviction in some cities).
• Eviction must be processed through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices, attend court hearings, and keep copies of all correspondence. | | **Maintenance of Records** | • Landlords must keep records of rent payments and maintenance requests. | • Request copies if needed for disputes. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If utilities are included, the landlord must maintain them in working order. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | --- #### Quick Steps If You Encounter Problems 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, emails, texts, photos, and a written log of incidents. 2. **Notify the Landlord in Writing** – Use certified mail or email with read receipt. 3. **Give Reasonable Time for Repairs** – Usually 7–10 days for major issues. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Many cities offer free mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 5. **File a Complaint** – If unresolved, file with TDHCA, TCHR, or HUD. 6. **Legal Counsel** – Consider a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid clinic. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, complaint filing. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Discrimination complaints. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair Housing Act enforcement. | | **Local Legal Aid Clinics** | Free or low‑cost legal advice. | | **Texas Apartment Association** | Tenant education and advocacy. | --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, fair treatment, and protection against discrimination. If your landlord violates these rights, you have several avenues for recourse—starting with written notice, then mediation, and finally legal action if necessary. Always keep thorough records and seek professional help when the situation escalates.
